name: i2c-tools
desc: Heterogeneous set of I2C tools for Linux
why: Scan buses, dump EEPROMs and poke chips over I2C, a direct door into the wires inside your machines.

brief.what_it_is: i2c-tools is a Linux package of command-line utilities for talking to I2C and SMBus devices through the kernel's I2C support. Per the wiki, it holds a bus probing tool, a chip dumper, register-level SMBus access helpers, EEPROM decoding scripts, EEPROM programming tools, and a Python module for SMBus access. The executables listed include i2cdetect, i2cdump, i2cget, i2cset, i2ctransfer, eeprog, decode-dimms, decode-edid, decode-vaio, ddcmon, and i2c-stub-from-dump. The tools take a bus number and chip address as input and print detected devices, register or EEPROM dumps, decoded contents, or write results.
brief.why_it_exists: The tools were split out of lm-sensors because, in the wiki's words, 'not all hardware monitoring chips are I2C devices, and not all I2C devices are hardware monitoring chips, so having everything in a single package was confusing and impractical.'
brief.how_it_works: The tools run in user space on top of the Linux kernel's I2C support, which the wiki says must be included in the kernel. The wiki says 'All versions of Linux are supported, as long as I2C support is included in the kernel.' The exact device-access mechanism is not described on the pages I read.

commands_seen.context: Wiki's command for checking out the latest stable code from the git repository.
Wiki's command for checking out the legacy 3.1 branch.

brief.install_notes: The wiki gives no install steps beyond the git clone commands and a download directory on kernel.org. Release tarballs are signed by Jean Delvare. The tools need I2C support in the Linux kernel. Access to real buses usually needs root or equivalent device permissions, but I did not confirm that on these pages. The Homebrew formula has no caveats text.
brief.standout: Most I2C probing tools work on one chip at a time. This package bundles bus scanning, raw register dumping, and EEPROM decoders for specific formats such as DIMM SPD and EDID monitor data in one toolkit. Its own scout note calls it 'a direct door into the wires inside your machines.'
brief.status: Maintained for the code, with the wiki archived. The git master branch has commits dated 2026, including 'i2c-tools: Enable cross compilation' and i2ctransfer changes in June 2026. The latest tagged release on the git page is v4.4, listed as about two years old. The wiki says 'This wiki has been archived and the content is no longer updated.' I did not fetch the README, so I did not check the release notes.
brief.caveats: The homepage is an archived, obsolete wiki page, so its setup and usage details may be outdated. The git listing and wiki point to the kernel.org repository as the current source. Only Linux is supported, and I2C support must be enabled in the kernel. I did not find a license statement. The README was not fetched, so the Homebrew formula's description may differ from the upstream text. Hardware access can affect real chips, and the pages I read do not describe safety limits.

judge.reason: It opens a direct window into the I2C bus inside your machine, letting you inspect and poke devices and decode real EEPROM formats like DIMM SPD and EDID.

entry.title: i2c-tools
entry.tldr: Command-line tools for scanning I2C buses, dumping chip registers, and decoding the EEPROMs inside your RAM sticks and monitor.
entry.deeper_look:
I2C is a two-wire bus that sits inside nearly every computer, running between chips that never show up as files or network ports. i2c-tools talks to those chips from user space through the Linux kernel's I2C support. You give it a bus number and a chip address, and it prints what answers: detected devices, register or EEPROM dumps, or the result of a write.

The package is a toolkit rather than a single program. `i2cdetect` probes a bus, `i2cdump` dumps a chip, and `i2cget` and `i2cset` read and write single registers. `i2ctransfer` handles raw transfers. `eeprog` programs EEPROMs. Several decoders turn raw bytes into something readable: `decode-dimms` for memory module data, `decode-edid` for monitor identification, and `decode-vaio` for Sony Vaio laptops. `i2c-stub-from-dump` is also included, but the brief does not say how it is used.

The tools were split out of lm-sensors because, in the wiki's words, "not all hardware monitoring chips are I2C devices, and not all I2C devices are hardware monitoring chips, so having everything in a single package was confusing and impractical." The idea underneath is that a lot of your hardware has a small, quiet management channel, and with the right address you can read it.
entry.install:
brew install i2c-tools
# Linux only: the kernel must have I2C support enabled. Real buses usually need root or device permissions (not confirmed in the brief). You need a machine with I2C buses to do anything useful.

try_this.what_happens: Shows the options for scanning an I2C bus for responding devices.
Shows how to dump the registers of a chip given a bus number and address.
Shows how to decode the memory module EEPROM data on your machine.

entry.whats_unique: Most I2C probing tools handle one chip at a time. This one bundles bus scanning, raw register access, and decoders for formats like DIMM SPD and EDID monitor data in one toolkit.
entry.caveats: Linux only, needs kernel I2C support, and the archived wiki may be outdated. Writing to real chips can affect hardware, and the pages I read describe no safety limits.
